nodes.name: Weighted ensemble
nodes.definition: An ensemble whose prediction is a weighted average of member predictions, with weights learned on validation data.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Ensemble diversity
nodes.definition: The degree to which ensemble members make different errors.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Data parallelism
nodes.definition: Replicating the full model on each device and having each replica process a different part of the data.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Model parallelism
nodes.definition: Splitting one model's parameters and computation across several devices that cooperate on the same batch.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Multi-GPU distributed training
nodes.definition: Training one model with several accelerators working together on each step.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Synchronous training
nodes.definition: Data-parallel training in which gradients from all replicas are averaged and applied identically, keeping weights equal at all times.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Sharding (model partitioning)
nodes.definition: Splitting one model instance's variables and computation across multiple devices.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Horizontal partitioning
nodes.definition: Each device runs a different set of layers.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Vertical partitioning
nodes.definition: Each layer's weight tensors are split across all devices; each device computes a slice of every layer.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Replica groups (figure 18.2)
nodes.definition: Eight devices organised as two model replicas of four devices each, each replica fed a local batch.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Multi-GPU speedup and scaling efficiency
nodes.definition: Speedup S(N) = T(1)/T(N); efficiency E(N) = S(N)/N.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: LayoutMap
nodes.definition: A dictionary-like mapping from variable paths to per-dimension sharding tuples over a device mesh.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Variable path
nodes.definition: A string identifier of a model variable, such as "sequential/dense_1/kernel", made of the model name, layer name and weight name.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: NamedSharding and PartitionSpec
nodes.definition: JAX's description of how an array is distributed: a device Mesh with named axes plus a PartitionSpec listing, per array dimension, which mesh axis it is split along (or None for replicated).
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Data prefetching with tf.data
nodes.definition: Preparing upcoming batches in the background while the accelerator processes the current batch, via dataset.prefetch(buffer_size).
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Tensor Processing Unit (TPU)
nodes.definition: Google's application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for deep learning, available on Google Cloud and Colab.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Step fusing (steps_per_execution)
nodes.definition: Running several training steps within a single device execution, set in Keras with compile(..., steps_per_execution=N).
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Large-batch training and learning rate
nodes.definition: Training with very large batches (e.g. >10,000 samples) to saturate accelerators, increasing the learning rate to compensate.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Numerical precision
nodes.definition: The number of bits used to store a number, which sets how finely values can be represented.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Floating-point encoding (sign, exponent, mantissa)
nodes.definition: A float is stored as a sign bit, a biased exponent, and a mantissa; its value is (−1)^s · 2^(e − bias) · (1.m)_2.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Non-uniform spacing of floats
nodes.definition: Each power-of-two interval [2^N, 2^(N+1)) contains the same number of representable floats, so spacing grows proportionally with magnitude.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Integer encodings (uint8, int32)
nodes.definition: Fixed-width binary representations of whole numbers with uniform spacing of 1.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: float16 (half precision)
nodes.definition: 16-bit IEEE float with 1 sign, 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Keras dtype policy
nodes.definition: A global setting controlling the dtypes Keras layers use for variables and computation.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: variable_dtype vs compute_dtype
nodes.definition: A Keras layer's storage dtype for weights and its dtype for computation, which can differ.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Loss scaling (introduced)
nodes.definition: Multiplying the loss by a large factor so float16 gradients don't underflow, then dividing the gradients by the same factor before the update.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Dynamic loss scaling (LossScaleOptimizer)
nodes.definition: Automatically adjusting the loss scale during training, as done by `keras.optimizers.LossScaleOptimizer`.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: float8 training
nodes.definition: Training in which some computations (mainly matmuls in Dense/EinsumDense/Embedding) run in 8-bit floating point, with per-tensor rescaling.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: int8 quantization
nodes.definition: Converting float tensors (weights and, at run time, activations) to 8-bit integers plus scale factors so that matmuls can run in integer arithmetic.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Abs-max scaling
nodes.definition: Choosing a tensor's quantization scale as the int range maximum (127) divided by the tensor's maximum absolute value.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Linearity of matmul
nodes.definition: Scaling either input of a matmul by a scalar scales the output by the same scalar.
nodes.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

nodes.name: Quantization error
nodes.definition: The difference between the quantized computation's output and the full-precision output, caused by rounding inputs to the integer grid.

nodes.name: Model as static (interpolative) database
nodes.definition: The view that a trained deep learning model stores patterns from its training data in fixed parameters and can only retrieve and interpolate them.

nodes.name: Adaptation to novelty
nodes.definition: The ability to handle situations not represented in prior experience.

nodes.name: In-context learning
nodes.definition: An LLM's apparent ability to pick up a task from examples in its prompt without weight updates.

nodes.name: Novelty vs. difficulty
nodes.definition: The claim that an LLM's ability to solve a problem depends on how familiar it is (how close to training data), not on how complex it is.

nodes.name: ARC-style puzzle
nodes.definition: A grid-based reasoning task in which a few input/output demonstration pairs illustrate a transformation rule that must be applied to a new test input.

nodes.name: Patching failures one prompt at a time
nodes.definition: Fixing a model's known failures by adding human-written corrections for the specific failing prompts to its training data.
aliases: Patching failures one prompt at a time

nodes.name: Adversarial example
nodes.definition: An input crafted, usually by a small perturbation, so that a model misclassifies it while a human sees no meaningful change.

nodes.name: Brittleness / sensitivity to input presentation
nodes.definition: The tendency of deep learning models to change their output under small changes in how an input is presented, even when the meaning is unchanged.

nodes.name: Prompt engineering
nodes.definition: Formulating LLM prompts to maximize performance on a task; in the book's interpretation, a trial-and-error search through latent space for the best lookup query.

nodes.name: Prompt as a database address
nodes.definition: The view that a prompt selects a location in the LLM's store of interpolable knowledge and programs, and the output is what is stored there.

nodes.name: Alice in Wonderland riddle
nodes.definition: 'Alice has N brothers and she also has M sisters. How many sisters does Alice's brother have?' Answer: M + 1.

nodes.name: Generalizable vs. interpolative programs
nodes.definition: A generalizable program gives correct results for all valid inputs; an interpolative program, as learned by deep learning, approximates the input-output mapping near its training examples.

nodes.name: Expressivity vs. learnability
nodes.definition: Whether a network that solves a task exists (expressivity) vs. whether training can find it from available data (learnability).

nodes.name: Anthropomorphizing models
nodes.definition: Attributing human understanding, intentions or experience to a model.

nodes.name: Theory of mind (and projecting it onto models)
nodes.definition: Our tendency to attribute intentions, beliefs and knowledge to things around us.
aliases: Theory of mind (and projecting it onto models)

nodes.name: Shortcuts to fit training data
nodes.definition: Models fit training labels with whatever features work, including spurious ones, rather than the concept humans intend.

nodes.name: 'Scale is all you need'
nodes.definition: The view that making models bigger and training them on more data will overcome deep learning's limitations and lead to general intelligence.

nodes.name: Deep learning as curve fitting
nodes.definition: Deep learning fits parametric curves (functions with many parameters) to datasets via gradient descent.

nodes.name: Automaton vs. intelligent agent
nodes.definition: An automaton executes fixed input-to-output behavior; an intelligent agent adapts its behavior to new situations.

nodes.name: Confounder features
nodes.definition: Features correlated with the target in the training data that don't actually determine it.

nodes.name: Behavioral program
nodes.definition: A set of instructions that makes an organism reactive to its environment ('If this happens, then do that'), linking sensory inputs to motor controls.

nodes.name: Evolution as search over behavior space
nodes.definition: Natural selection, acting on DNA that is decoded into neural wiring, explores the space of possible behaviors by random variation and selective retention.
aliases: Evolution as search over behavior space

nodes.name: Automaton
nodes.definition: A system that executes a fixed program crafted for specific situations, without the ability to adapt on the fly to novel ones.

nodes.name: Intelligence vs. automation
nodes.definition: Automation executes fixed programs for anticipated contexts. Intelligence is the ability to adapt on the fly to novel, unexpected situations.

nodes.name: Fluid intelligence
nodes.definition: The capacity to reason through and solve novel problems, as opposed to applying stored knowledge.

nodes.name: Known unknowns
nodes.definition: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data.

nodes.name: Information conversion ratio
nodes.definition: How efficiently a system converts the information it has (known situations, experience, priors) into an operational area, the set of situations it can handle.

nodes.name: Intelligence (author's definition)
nodes.definition: The ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in the face of an uncertain, ever-changing future.

nodes.name: Abstraction (modular, reusable)
nodes.definition: A compact unit of knowledge mined from past experience that can be quickly repurposed to handle novel situations.

nodes.name: Spectrum of generalization
nodes.definition: A scale ordering systems by how broadly they generalize: from automaton-like local generalization, through broader generalization, to extreme generalization.

nodes.name: Selection for adaptability
nodes.definition: The evolutionary shift in which brains were optimized for adaptability and generality themselves, rather than for fitness to a fixed set of situations.

nodes.name: Broad generalization
nodes.definition: The ability to deal with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations the system was not trained to handle and that its creators could not have anticipated.

nodes.name: Kaleidoscope hypothesis
nodes.definition: Our experience of the world seems endlessly complex and novel, but everything is similar to everything else: a relatively small number of unique atoms of meaning, recombined, describes everything.

nodes.name: Analogy
nodes.definition: Making sense of something new by mapping it onto past experience and abstract concepts, preserving relevant structure.

nodes.name: Atoms of meaning
nodes.definition: The relatively small set of unique building blocks needed to describe the universe, from which everything is a recombination.

nodes.name: Isomorphism (in physical reality)
nodes.definition: A structure-preserving correspondence between two systems; the author says physical reality itself is full of them.

nodes.name: Abstraction acquisition
nodes.definition: Efficiently extracting compact, reusable abstractions from a stream of experience or data by identifying underlying structures, principles or invariants.

nodes.name: On-the-fly recombination
nodes.definition: Efficiently selecting and recombining abstractions in novel ways to model new problems and situations, even ones far removed from past experience.

nodes.name: Efficiency as the measure of intelligence
nodes.definition: Intelligence is determined by how efficiently abstractions are acquired from limited experience and recombined to deal with uncertainty and novelty.
aliases: Efficiency as the measure of intelligence

nodes.name: Shortcut rule
nodes.definition: If you optimize for one success metric, you achieve it at the expense of everything in the system the metric doesn't cover, taking every available shortcut.

nodes.name: Task-specific skill vs. intelligence
nodes.definition: Skill is performance on a particular task; intelligence is the ability to adapt to novelty and efficiently acquire skills at never-before-seen tasks.

nodes.name: 'Buying' skill with data or hardcoded knowledge
nodes.definition: Increasing a system's skill on a fixed task by adding more training data or more human-written rules, without improving its ability to generalize.
aliases: 'Buying' skill with data or hardcoded knowledge

nodes.name: Proxy task
nodes.definition: A task chosen as a target because it is believed to require some underlying capability (here, chess as a proxy for cognition).

nodes.name: Generalization power
nodes.definition: How much skill a system can extract from a given amount of task-relevant information (priors plus experience), particularly on situations unlike those it has seen.

nodes.name: Priors (prior knowledge)
nodes.definition: Knowledge a system has before any task experience: innate knowledge in humans, built-in design in AI systems.

nodes.name: Core Knowledge priors
nodes.definition: The knowledge systems humans are born with, assumed to be the only prior knowledge needed for ARC-AGI.

nodes.name: ARC Prize
nodes.definition: A yearly competition, run by the nonprofit ARC Prize Foundation (Chollet and Mike Knoop, 2024), with a prize pool over $1 million in 2024 for progress on ARC-AGI.

nodes.name: Test-time adaptation (TTA)
nodes.definition: Methods where an AI system actively reasons or learns during the test itself, using the information in the specific problem.

nodes.name: Test-time training
nodes.definition: Adjusting some of a model's parameters with gradient descent on the examples given in a test task.

nodes.name: Program synthesis (as test-time search)
nodes.definition: Searching a space of symbolic, verifiable programs at test time for one that matches the task's examples.

nodes.name: Benchmark saturation via memorization
nodes.definition: A benchmark stops being informative when models reach near-ceiling scores, often because test content can be covered by memorized training data.

nodes.name: Brute-force search as a shortcut
nodes.definition: Exhaustively trying candidate solutions with large compute until one fits, which can solve tasks without intelligence.

nodes.name: Binary vs. graded benchmarks
nodes.definition: A benchmark is binary when scores cluster near zero or near the top, showing whether a capability is present but not how much of it.

nodes.name: ARC-AGI-2
nodes.definition: The second version of ARC-AGI, in development since 2022 and released in March 2025, keeping the format but with harder, less brute-forcible tasks.

nodes.name: Intelligence as efficiency
nodes.definition: The view that intelligence is measured by how few resources (data, compute) a system needs to reach a result, not by raw capability.

nodes.name: Value-centric analogy / abstraction
nodes.definition: Abstraction formed by comparing instances with a continuous similarity (distance) function, clustering them, and merging clusters into prototypes.

nodes.name: Program-centric (structure-centric) analogy
nodes.definition: Abstraction formed by finding exactly matching structure across instances (introduced here, developed on p.610-611).

nodes.name: K-means clustering
nodes.definition: An unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by alternately assigning points to their nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as cluster means.

nodes.name: Subgraph isomorphism
nodes.definition: An exact structure-preserving match between a subgraph of one graph and another graph.

nodes.name: Cognition as a blend of both poles
nodes.definition: The thesis that all thought interleaves value-centric and program-centric abstraction.
aliases: Cognition as a blend of both poles

nodes.name: Spectrum between the two poles
nodes.definition: Each pole can partly emulate the other: continuous models can fit discrete programs, and discrete programs can compute continuous functions.

nodes.name: Genetic programming
nodes.definition: A form of program synthesis that uses evolutionary search over programs.

nodes.name: Hybrid (neurosymbolic) AI system
nodes.definition: A system combining learned continuous models (deep learning modules) with discrete, symbol-manipulating programs.
aliases: Blend of algorithmic and geometric modules

nodes.name: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
nodes.definition: A tree search algorithm that grows a search tree selectively, steering exploration toward promising branches and evaluating positions by simulation or a learned evaluator.

nodes.name: Programming primitives for neural networks
nodes.definition: Discrete building blocks such as if branches, while statements, variable creation, long-term disk storage, sorting operators, and data structures (lists, graphs, hash tables).

nodes.name: Combinatorial explosion
nodes.definition: The very fast growth of the number of possible programs as specification complexity or the vocabulary of primitives increases.

nodes.name: Deep-learning-guided program search
nodes.definition: Using a learned model to prioritize which candidate programs or program fragments to explore, instead of enumerating them blindly.
aliases: Program synthesis guided by program-space intuition

nodes.name: Lifelong learning and reuse across tasks
nodes.definition: Accumulating knowledge and components across a sequence of tasks and reusing them rather than training each model from scratch.
aliases: Lifelong learning and reuse across tasks

nodes.name: Compositional generalization / recombination
nodes.definition: The ability to combine known functions into new programs on the fly to handle novel situations.

nodes.name: Global library of abstract subroutines
nodes.definition: A shared, persistent store of reusable program components (geometric and algorithmic) built from the cumulative experience of all AI instances.

nodes.name: Perpetual meta-learner
nodes.definition: A system that quickly grows task-specific models across a variety of tasks, using and extending a library of reusable primitives.

nodes.name: Abstracting recurring subroutines
nodes.definition: Recognizing that similar subroutines were developed for several tasks and creating a general, reusable version.

nodes.name: AI summer (and winter)
nodes.definition: A period of intense interest, investment, and hype in AI; historically followed by disappointment and funding cuts (AI winter).

nodes.name: Deep learning as chained geometric transformations
nodes.definition: Inputs and targets are points in vector spaces; each layer applies a simple geometric transformation; the model is their composition, mapping input space to target space.
aliases: Deep learning as chained geometric transformations

nodes.name: Simplicity plus scale
nodes.definition: The observation that large parametric models trained with gradient descent on many examples suffice for perception and NLP.

nodes.name: Meaning as pairwise relationships captured by distance
nodes.definition: The assumption that meaning derives from relationships between things, and that these can be represented by distances in a vector space.
aliases: Meaning as pairwise relationships captured by distance

nodes.name: Why 'neural network' is a misleading name
nodes.definition: The name is historical, from connectionism's graphs; modern models are neither neural nor networks.
aliases: Why 'neural network' is a misleading name

nodes.name: Enabling factors of the deep learning revolution
nodes.definition: Algorithmic innovations, large datasets, cheap parallel hardware, and a software stack, accumulating over time.
aliases: Enabling factors of the deep learning revolution

nodes.name: GPU acceleration
nodes.definition: Running tensor operations on massively parallel processors such as NVIDIA GPUs.

nodes.name: Validation-set overfitting
nodes.definition: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning.

nodes.name: Modality-to-architecture mapping (Table 20.1)
nodes.definition: Default architecture choices per input/output modality.

nodes.name: Matching last-layer activation and loss to the task
nodes.definition: The task type determines the size and activation of the last layer and the loss.
aliases: Matching last-layer activation and loss to the task

nodes.name: Stacking RNN layers with return_sequences
nodes.definition: Every RNN layer except the last returns its full output sequence so the next RNN layer receives a sequence.

nodes.name: GlobalMaxPooling1D for sequences
nodes.definition: Reduces a (batch, seq_length, dim) tensor to (batch, dim) by taking the maximum over the sequence axis.

nodes.name: Anthropomorphizing models
nodes.definition: Attributing human-like understanding to models whose competence comes from statistical patterns.

nodes.name: arXiv preprints
nodes.definition: Research papers posted publicly on the arXiv open-access server, typically before peer review.
aliases: Open research and its signal-to-noise problem

nodes.name: Keras ecosystem
nodes.definition: The documentation, guides, examples, source repositories and related libraries (such as KerasHub) around Keras.
